questions.q: Which earlier name for antiphospholipid syndrome is printed at the head of the chapter?
opts: Acquired phospholipid anaemia syndrome
Autoimmune platelet activation syndrome
Antiphospholipid anticoagulant deficiency
Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLA)
questions.exp: The heading notes the syndrome was earlier called antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLA). (Book p466)

questions.q: What proportion of SLE cases is printed as antiphospholipid-syndrome positive?
opts: One-third of SLE cases
One-tenth of SLE cases
All SLE cases
None of the SLE cases
questions.exp: The chapter notes that one-third of SLE cases are APS positive. (Book p466)

questions.q: A patient with SLE is found to have antiphospholipid antibodies and asks about the thrombotic tendency. Which pattern does the source describe?
opts: Increased arterial dissection risk without thrombosis
Increased susceptibility to thrombus formation, venous more than arterial
Increased susceptibility to haemorrhage, venous more than arterial
Increased capillary fragility with purpura only
questions.exp: In the complications-of-SLE note, APS is described as increasing susceptibility to thrombus formation, with venous more than arterial events. (Book p466)

questions.q: Which complication listed under SLE involves medium vessels of the gut and CNS?
opts: Glomerular disease
Complications of immunosuppression
Vasculitis
Accelerated atherosclerosis
questions.exp: The SLE complications note lists accelerated atherosclerosis, glomerular disease (class III/IV lupus nephritis), complications of immunosuppression, vasculitis of medium vessels (GIT/CNS) and APS. (Book p466)

questions.q: How does the source divide primary and secondary APS?
opts: About 90% primary; secondary disease does not exist
About 10% primary; the rest are secondary to malignancy
All cases are secondary to SLE
About 50% primary, associated with HLA DR4 and DRw53; at least 50% secondary, most commonly from SLE
questions.exp: APS: 50% of cases are primary, associated with HLA DR4 and HLA DRw53; 50% or more are secondary, most commonly due to SLE (one-third of APS). (Book p466)

questions.q: Which HLA-disease pairing is printed in the side note beside the APS epidemiology block?
opts: HLA DR3 positivity is linked to Sjogren syndrome and SLE; the most common cause of secondary Sjogren is rheumatoid arthritis
HLA DR4 positivity is linked to Sjogren syndrome and SLE
HLA DR5 positivity is linked to Sjogren syndrome
No HLA association is noted for Sjogren syndrome
questions.exp: The side note states the most common cause of secondary Sjogren is RA and that HLA DR3 positivity is associated with Sjogren syndrome and SLE. (Book p466)

questions.q: Against which targets are the antiphospholipid antibodies directed according to the pathophysiology diagram?
opts: Endothelial nitric oxide synthase alone
Phospholipid-binding proteins: beta-2 glycoprotein I, the prothrombin-phosphatidylserine complex and annexin
Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa alone
Factor VIII alone
questions.exp: Antibodies are directed against phospholipid-binding proteins: beta-2 glycoprotein I, the prothrombin-phosphatidylserine complex and annexin, with platelet surface proteins shown alongside. (Book p466)

questions.q: Which platelet count range is printed alongside the raised propensity to thrombosis?
opts: Thrombocytosis above one lakh
A normal platelet count is mandatory
Thrombocytopenia of about 50,000 to one lakh
Thrombocytopenia below 10,000
questions.exp: The pathway ends in thrombocytopenia (50,000 to one lakh) with an increased propensity to thrombosis. (Book p466)

questions.q: Which downstream mechanisms are printed after antigen-antibody complex formation?
opts: Platelet inhibition and fibrinolysis leading to bleeding
Complement inhibition with no thrombotic tendency
Purely arterial vasospasm without thrombosis
Increased affinity for platelets and complement activation, plus reduced inhibition of coagulation factors, leading to thrombosis
questions.exp: The diagram shows the Ag-Ab complex with increased affinity for platelets, activation of the complement cascade, thrombocytopenia with a raised thrombotic tendency, and reduced inhibition of coagulation factors progressing to thrombosis. (Book p466)

questions.q: What are the two hits printed in the APS model?
opts: First hit: antibody causing endothelial injury; second hit: oestrogen, smoking, obesity or other prothrombotic states
First hit: infection; second hit: malignancy
First hit: platelet antibodies; second hit: complement deficiency
First hit: trauma; second hit: immobilisation only
questions.exp: The two hits are the antibody causing endothelial injury and a second hit such as oestrogen, smoking, obesity or other prothrombotic states. (Book p467)

questions.q: A young woman presents with an unprovoked venous thrombosis and thrombophilia testing is planned. Which ranking of causes does the source print?
opts: Acquired and inherited causes are equally common
Acquired: antiphospholipid syndrome is the most common; inherited: factor V Leiden mutation
Acquired: malignancy is the most common; inherited: protein C deficiency
Inherited: factor V Leiden is more common than any acquired cause
questions.exp: The most common cause of thrombophilia is acquired (APS), greater than inherited factor V Leiden mutation. (Book p467)

questions.q: How is the thrombosis spectrum ranked in the clinical-features list?
opts: Stroke more than DVT more than Budd-Chiari syndrome
Superficial thrombophlebitis more than DVT
DVT more than arterial thrombosis (stroke) more than Budd-Chiari syndrome
Budd-Chiari syndrome more than DVT more than stroke
questions.exp: Thrombosis: DVT is more common than arterial thrombosis (stroke), which is more common than Budd-Chiari syndrome. (Book p467)

questions.q: A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome presents with painful hepatomegaly and ascites, and later with a cerebral venous thrombosis. Which venous territories does the source name?
opts: Portal vein causing portal hypertension only
Renal vein causing nephrotic syndrome only
Upper-limb veins only
Hepatic vein causing Budd-Chiari syndrome and cerebral veins causing cortical vein thrombosis
questions.exp: Veins involved: hepatic vein gives Budd-Chiari syndrome and cerebral veins give cerebral venous thrombosis. (Book p467)

questions.q: Which organs are listed under microvascular APS involvement?
opts: Kidneys more than adrenals
Liver more than spleen
Skin more than joints
Heart more than lungs
questions.exp: Microvascular involvement affects the kidneys more than the adrenals. (Book p467)

questions.q: A young patient has livedo reticularis and an ischaemic stroke. Which syndrome does the source name?
opts: Fabry disease
Sneddon's syndrome
Susac syndrome
Eales disease
questions.exp: Sneddon's syndrome is listed with livedo reticularis and stroke in the APS clinical-features block. (Book p467)

questions.q: A young woman presents with hepatic vein thrombosis and antiphospholipid antibodies are considered. Which differential diagnosis does the source list?
opts: APS, sarcoidosis and amyloidosis
APS, malaria and leptospirosis
APS, polycythemia rubra vera and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
APS, Wilson disease and haemochromatosis
questions.exp: The note gives the differential for hepatic vein thrombosis as APS, polycythemia rubra vera and PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria). (Book p467)

questions.q: A young patient with antiphospholipid syndrome has an acute neurological deficit with a cranial nerve palsy and pyramidal weakness. Which stroke profile does the source highlight?
opts: Insidious onset with a purely sensory deficit
Stepwise progression with normal examination
Always haemorrhagic with coma
Acute onset, cranial nerve palsy and a pyramidal pattern of weakness
questions.exp: The note describes the stroke as acute in onset with cranial nerve palsy and a pyramidal pattern of weakness. (Book p467)

questions.q: What persistence requirement is printed for the Sapporo laboratory criteria?
opts: Any antibody positive twice, at least 12 weeks apart
A single positive antibody at any time
Three positive results within one week
Antibody positivity for five consecutive years
questions.exp: Laboratory criteria: any antibody positive twice over 12 weeks. (Book p467)

questions.q: Which assay is attached to anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies in the Sapporo criteria?
opts: Agglutination testing only
ELISA for IgG or IgM anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I
Indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells
Western blot only
questions.exp: Anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I (IgG/IgM) is detected by ELISA. (Book p467)

questions.q: Which anticardiolipin threshold and performance are printed?
opts: IgA above 40 units; described as specific
Any titre; described as neither sensitive nor specific
IgG or IgM above 40 units; described as sensitive
IgG or IgM above 4 units; described as specific
questions.exp: Anti-cardiolipin antibody (IgG/IgM >40 units) is described as sensitive. (Book p467)

questions.q: A patient has an unexplained prolonged aPTT and a positive lupus anticoagulant. How does the source characterise this test, and which assays are named?
opts: Sensitive but not specific: normal aPTT with a raised bleeding time
Both highly sensitive and specific: prolonged prothrombin time only
Of no diagnostic value in APS
Specific but not sensitive: raised aPTT and a raised dilute Russell's viper venom test (dRVVT)
questions.exp: Lupus anticoagulant is specific but not sensitive, with a raised aPTT and a raised dRVVT (diluted Russell's viper venom test). (Book p467)

questions.q: Which vascular event satisfies the clinical criterion for APS?
opts: A vascular event due to venous or arterial thrombosis
Any episode of vasovagal syncope
A bleed requiring transfusion
An isolated elevation of D-dimer
questions.exp: Clinical criteria: a vascular event due to venous or arterial thrombosis. (Book p468)

questions.q: Which obstetric criteria are printed for APS?
opts: Infertility alone

Any one miscarriage at or beyond 10 weeks, or three or more miscarriages before 10 weeks, or premature delivery before 34 weeks of a morphologically normal neonate due to pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or HELLP syndrome
Any two first-trimester losses with a chromosomal abnormality
Delivery before 37 weeks for any reason
questions.exp: Pregnancy criteria: one miscarriage ≥10 weeks, or ≥3 miscarriages before 10 weeks, or premature delivery <34 weeks of a morphologically normal neonate due to pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or HELLP syndrome. (Book p468)

questions.q: A woman with recurrent pregnancy loss after 10 weeks of gestation is evaluated for antiphospholipid syndrome. Which obstetric role does the source highlight?
opts: APS never causes pregnancy loss
APS causes loss only in the third trimester
APS is the most common cause of second-trimester abortion, that is loss after 10 weeks
APS only causes first-trimester loss
questions.exp: The note states APS is the most common cause of second-trimester abortion (after 10 weeks). (Book p468)

questions.q: A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome has chorea and a pansystolic murmur from mitral regurgitation. Which non-criteria manifestations does the source list?
opts: CNS: stroke only; cardiac: myocardial infarction only
CNS: dementia; cardiac: aortic stenosis
CNS: meningitis; cardiac: pericardial tamponade
CNS: chorea, epilepsy and migraine; cardiac: Libman-Sacks endocarditis and mitral regurgitation
questions.exp: Non-criteria APS: CNS shows chorea, epilepsy and migraine; cardiac shows Libman-Sacks endocarditis and MR. (Book p468)

questions.q: Which haematological manifestations are listed under non-criteria APS?
opts: Warm-antibody autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and Evan's syndrome
Cold agglutinin disease and sickle cell crisis
Iron-deficiency anaemia and thalassaemia trait
Aplastic anaemia and myelodysplasia
questions.exp: Hematological: warm-antibody autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and Evan's syndrome, with thrombocytopenia not significant enough to cause bleeding. (Book p468)

questions.q: A renal biopsy in a patient with antiphospholipid antibodies shows thrombotic microangiopathy. How does the source describe the renal lesion?
opts: Acute tubular necrosis from hypotension
APS nephropathy: thrombotic microangiopathy from microvascular involvement of the kidney
Immune-complex membranous nephropathy
Minimal-change disease
questions.exp: Renal: APS nephropathy is a thrombotic microangiopathy due to microvascular involvement of the kidney. (Book p468)

questions.q: A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome collapses in shock and livedo reticularis is noted over the legs. Which non-criteria entries explain these findings?
opts: Endocrine: diabetes insipidus; dermatological: vitiligo
Endocrine: hyperparathyroidism; dermatological: psoriasis
Endocrine: adrenal-vessel infarction with adrenal insufficiency; dermatological: venous obstruction and venular dilatation producing livedo reticularis
Endocrine: thyroiditis; dermatological: urticaria
questions.exp: Endocrine: infarction of adrenal vessels leads to adrenal insufficiency (shock); dermatological: venous obstruction with venular dilatation gives livedo reticularis. (Book p468)

questions.q: Which domains are listed under the clinical and laboratory columns of the APS domain table?
opts: Clinical: fever and rash; laboratory: ESR and CRP
Clinical: renal and hepatic; laboratory: complement and immunoglobulins
Clinical: neurologic and pulmonary; laboratory: imaging and biopsy
Clinical: macrovascular venous, macrovascular arterial, microvascular, obstetric, cardiac valve and haematology; laboratory: lupus anticoagulant test and other antibody tests
questions.exp: Domains: clinical domains 1-6 (macrovascular venous, macrovascular arterial, microvascular, obstetric, cardiac valve, haematology) and laboratory domains 7-8 (lupus anticoagulant test, other antibody tests). (Book p469)

questions.q: How is catastrophic APS defined in the note?
opts: Three or more organ systems involved within one week, with small-vessel involvement
One organ system involved over one year
Two organ systems over one month with large-vessel disease
Any thrombotic event with a positive antibody
questions.exp: Catastrophic APS: three or more organ systems involved within one week, with small vessels involved; presentations include thrombotic microangiopathy of the kidney and adrenal insufficiency. (Book p469)

questions.q: An asymptomatic adult with antiphospholipid antibodies but no events is reviewed. What does the source advise?
opts: Monthly intravenous immunoglobulin
No treatment is required
Lifelong warfarin
Dual antiplatelet therapy
questions.exp: Management: an asymptomatic adult requires no treatment. (Book p469)

questions.q: Which anticoagulation targets and regimens are printed for an adult with a thrombotic episode?
opts: Target INR 3.5-4.5 with warfarin alone for six weeks
Target INR 2.5-3 with a direct oral anticoagulant
Target INR 2.5-3 using heparin 5000 units three times daily subcutaneously or LMWH 60 mg twice daily, overlapped with warfarin continued lifelong
Target INR 1-1.5 with aspirin alone
questions.exp: To attain an INR of 2.5-3: heparin 5000 units TDS SC or LMWH 60 mg BD SC, with warfarin overlapped with heparin/LMWH and continued lifelong; the note adds there is no role for NOACs. (Book p469)

questions.q: A pregnant patient with known APS and a history of previous thrombosis asks about prophylaxis. What is printed?
opts: Warfarin throughout pregnancy
Aspirin alone for the first trimester only
No prophylaxis is required
Prophylactic low-dose aspirin plus heparin throughout pregnancy and for 6-12 weeks post-partum
questions.exp: Pregnancy management: prophylactic low-dose aspirin with heparin throughout pregnancy and for 6-12 weeks post-partum; warfarin is continued lifelong if APS is diagnosed. (Book p469)

questions.q: Which regimen is printed for catastrophic APS?
opts: Steroids plus intravenous immunoglobulin plus plasmapheresis
Warfarin alone
Aspirin plus clopidogrel
Cyclophosphamide pulses
questions.exp: Catastrophic APS is managed with steroids, IV Ig and plasmapheresis. (Book p469)

questions.q: A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome on warfarin asks whether a direct oral anticoagulant can replace it. Which caution does the source print?
opts: NOACs replace warfarin after one year
There is no role for new oral anticoagulants (NOACs) in APS
NOACs are the first-line choice in all APS patients
NOACs are preferred in pregnancy
questions.exp: The note states there is no role for new oral anticoagulants (NOACs) in APS. (Book p469)

units.title: 1. APS Overview, SLE Association & Pathophysiology
units.guide:
The chapter opens with the older APLA terminology and the size of the APS/SLE overlap.
A note lists the complications of SLE that set the stage for APS.
Pathophysiology then traces antigen-antibody complexes to thrombosis.

units.title: 2. Two-Hit Model, Clinical Features & Thrombophilia
units.guide:
The two-hit model separates the antibody from the prothrombotic co-trigger.
Thrombosis is then ranked by site, with venous disease leading and Budd-Chiari next.
Microvascular involvement and Sneddon syndrome close the clinical list.

units.title: 3. Sapporo Classification & Clinical Criteria
units.guide:
The Sapporo laboratory criteria require persistence of antibodies over 12 weeks.
Each antibody is then characterised as sensitive or specific, with its own assay.
The clinical criteria span vascular events and the obstetric definitions.

units.title: 4. Non-Criteria APS, Catastrophic APS & Management
units.guide:
Non-criteria manifestations are mapped organ by organ, outside the classification.
Catastrophic APS is defined by speed, small-vessel involvement and organ count.
Management then separates the asymptomatic carrier from thrombosis, pregnancy and catastrophe.
